content: Antiretroviral drugs are essential for both treating and preventing HIV infection. The implementation of new treatment recommendations at a national scale depends not only on the availability of additional drug products but also on the manufacturing lead time, which can influence the speed of adoption by healthcare programs. For children under three years of age, first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens are recommended, while third-line ART regimens are also addressed for specific cases. Transitioning to preferred regimens and formulations is emphasized, with guidelines recommending once-daily fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) to streamline procurement, supply chain management, logistics, and patient adherence. National programs must address logistical and programmatic factors to select optimal formulations. It is advised that national programs limit the procurement of pediatric ARV products to those listed in the Optimal Pediatric Formulary by the Inter-Agency Task Team (IATT) on Prevention and Treatment of HIV in Pregnant Women, Mothers, and Children. Adhering to the IATT Optimal Formulary, which aligns with WHO recommendations, simplifies the supply chain and stabilizes the global supply of pediatric ARV drugs. Certain pediatric formulations should no longer be procured. Stavudine (d4T) is no longer recommended due to its cumulative mitochondrial toxicity, and children currently on d4T-based regimens should transition to preferred pediatric ART regimens. Similarly, didanosine (ddI) is no longer recommended as an alternative nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) in pediatric second-line regimens due to its toxicity, lower efficacy, and inconvenient dosing requirements. When available, age-appropriate FDCs are preferred for any recommended regimen. Dispersible tablets, also known as tablets for oral solution, are the preferred solid oral formulations, while oral liquid formulations should be avoided when solid oral dosage forms are available. For example, FDCs of abacavir (ABC) and lamivudine (3TC) in dispersible scored tablets are recommended as the preferred option in the Optimal Pediatric Formulary. Additionally, three formulations of lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) are available for young children: heat-stable tablets for children over 10 kg who can swallow whole tablets, oral pellets to be taken with soft food, and oral liquid formulations for infants. The IATT has developed a fact sheet on administering the new oral pellet dosage form of LPV/r to address challenges in ensuring the availability of pediatric ARV formulations. The IATT also provides guidance on optimal ARV drug products for children to promote a secure and sustainable supply. Introducing new ARV drug formulations for adults, adolescents, and children is a complex process that requires careful planning. Policymakers and procurement and supply management (PSM) managers must consider factors such as patent restrictions, product registration, forecasted demand, and the impact on existing medicines. For example, faster adoption of new products may lead to stock-outs if procurement plans are not adjusted, while slower adoption could result in expired stock. PSM managers should closely monitor consumption and develop risk mitigation strategies, such as collaborating with suppliers for flexible delivery schedules. The introduction of new products also requires consideration of procurement budgets, shelf life, storage requirements, and production status. For products in low demand, collaboration with neighboring countries or global pooled procurement mechanisms may be necessary to achieve viable order volumes for manufacturers. Laboratory and diagnostic services must also be strengthened to support the implementation of these guidelines. This includes ensuring access to high-quality diagnostics, strategic placement of testing platforms, and expanding laboratory networks to support decentralized and integrated testing services. Viral load testing is recommended for monitoring treatment response and diagnosing treatment failure, with dried blood spot samples being a viable option to increase access. As viral load testing becomes more widely available, the demand for CD4 count testing is expected to decrease, but CD4 testing will still be needed for baseline risk assessments and other clinical purposes. Decentralizing diagnostic services to point-of-care settings requires the use of high-quality, reliable diagnostic tests, supervision of testing quality, and effective supply chain management. In summary, the successful implementation of new antiretroviral treatment guidelines requires careful planning, coordination, and resource allocation across multiple levels of healthcare systems.
